understanding the molecular basis of cellular transformation by adenoviral oncoprotein E1A and how E1A hijacked cellular transcriptional machinery.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

E1A has evolved to be a highly efficient oncoprotein that subverts cellular control mechanisms by simultaneously binding to CBP and the retinolblastoma protein (pRB) and thereby deregulating cellular transcription.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
E1A is a master switch that can control cellular transcription and cell growth by competing for binding to cellular proteins.
E1A is a master regulator of the transcription machinery by competing for binding to transcription factors and coactivators.

E1A is an intrinsically unstructured protein that binds to the TAZ2 domain of CBP through a local folding event and that this binding event is mutually exclusive with the binding of the N-terminal transactivating domain of p53.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have determined the structural basis by which the adenoviral oncoprotein E1A subverts cellular control mechanisms by competing with essential cellular transcription factors for binding the cellular transcriptional coactivator CBP/p300.
the E1A protein is able to bind to the TAZ2 domain of p300/CBP in the absence of p53 or the retinobastoma protein.
E1A is able to compete with other cellular transcription factors for binding CBP, thereby hijacking the cellular transcription machinery for its own purposes.
